title: Amazon Signed a Multibillion-Dollar Deal With a 175-Year-Old Glassmaker. Is Fiber the Next AI Bottleneck?
excerpt: Amazon’s June 8 agreement with a company founded in 1851 says something important about the newest AI systems: their performance depends on more than process...
content_html:
Amazon's June 8 agreement with a company founded in 1851 says something important about the newest AI systems: their performance depends on more than processors. Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) signed a multiyear, multibillion-dollar deal with Corning Incorporated (NYSE:GLW) for optical fiber, cable, and connectivity products. Corning expects the work to support about 1,000 jobs in North Carolina. As Amazon pushes annual capital spending toward roughly $220 billion, fiber is moving from a background component to a strategic AI input.

Photo from Meta Platforms

The logic here is physical, as accelerators can process data only as quickly as networks deliver it, and large clusters require dense optical connections inside facilities and between campuses. Corning Incorporated (NYSE:GLW) gains scale, visibility, and a marquee customer whose AWS revenue grew 36.7% in the second quarter. Its separate agreement to provide Meta with up to $6 billion of products reinforces the bull case that optical infrastructure is becoming a durable bottleneck rather than a one-customer windfall.

Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) benefits by securing supply and shaping products for its own architecture. That can protect deployment schedules when every hyperscaler is chasing the same components. Yet the contract also highlights the cost of staying competitive. Amazon must spend before AI utilization and revenue fully arrive, and fiber commitments do not guarantee attractive returns on the servers they connect. A slowdown in cloud demand could leave more infrastructure underused.

Corning carries the opposite risk, because huge commitments can justify manufacturing expansion, but customer concentration increases bargaining power on the buyer's side. The company must add capacity without assuming today's extraordinary spending persists indefinitely. Glass and cable are also more cyclical and capital intensive than software, so strong volume does not automatically produce equally strong margins. The opportunity is real, but execution determines how much value the supplier retains.

Hedge-fund holder counts increased for both companies. Amazon was held by 369 funds in the second quarter, up from 353, while Corning ownership rose to 99 funds from 91. Arrowstreet Capital increased its Amazon position 24% to 40.3 million shares, while Polar Capital reduced its Corning stake 9% but still owned about 3.1 million shares. As of August 14, 16.8 million Corning shares were sold short, equal to 1.95% of the float and 1.6 days of average volume. That modest snapshot shows limited reported short positioning in Corning. Separately, the Amazon agreement supports the view that reliable optical bandwidth may help determine how quickly Amazon can turn its giant AI budget into usable computing capacity.
